slides.title: Arithmetic Progressions
bullets: Class 10 — NIOS Mathematics
Chapter 7
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. Today we move from quadratic equations to sequences — specifically to the simplest kind of sequence, where each term differs from the previous by a fixed amount. We'll meet the n-th term and sum formulas, and apply them to short word problems.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Recognise an AP and identify a and d.
Use a_n = a + (n − 1) d to find a specific term.
Use S_n = (n/2)(2 a + (n − 1) d) and S_n = (n/2)(a + l) to compute sums.
Compute the arithmetic mean and insert n means.
Solve short word problems modelled by APs.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each objective; ask students which they feel least sure about and weight the lesson accordingly.

slides.title: Sequences and series
bullets: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers a_1, a_2, a_3, ….
A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence.
S_n = a_1 + a_2 + … + a_n is the partial sum of the first n terms.
Sequences may be defined by a closed-form rule (a_n = 2 n) or recursively (Fibonacci).
Today we focus on sequences with constant successive differences.
slides.speaker_notes: Distinguish 'sequence' (list) from 'series' (sum) carefully — a common student conflation.

slides.title: Arithmetic progression — definition
bullets: An AP is a sequence with a_2 − a_1 = a_3 − a_2 = … = d.
d is the common difference; a (or a_1) is the first term.
AP form: a, a + d, a + 2 d, a + 3 d, ….
d > 0: increasing; d < 0: decreasing; d = 0: constant.
To check, compute successive differences and verify all equal.
slides.speaker_notes: Use the spot-the-AP cards to anchor each example. Pause on the constant sequence — it is an AP.

slides.title: Spot the AP
bullets: 1, 4, 9, 16 → diffs 3, 5, 7 ✗ not AP (squares).
2, 4, 8, 16 → diffs 2, 4, 8 ✗ not AP (powers of 2).
slides.speaker_notes: Cover the squares case carefully — it tempts students to call any pattern an AP.

slides.title: n-th term of an AP
bullets: Workhorse formula: a_n = a + (n − 1) d.
Used to find a specific term, the position of a known term, or d.
Which term of 7, 13, 19, … is 205? Solve 7 + 6 (n − 1) = 205 → n = 34.
Common slip: writing 'a + n d' instead of 'a + (n − 1) d'.
slides.speaker_notes: Drill the (n − 1) carefully — the most common slip in AP problems.

slides.title: Sum of the first n terms
bullets: Form 2: S_n = (n/2)(a + l), where l = a_n is the last term.
Derived by Gauss's forwards + backwards pairing trick.
Use Form 1 when only a, d, n are known; Form 2 when a and l are known.
slides.speaker_notes: Long-derive Form 1 live on the board using the Gauss trick; that derivation is what students should remember.

slides.title: Worked: sum of the first 30 terms of 2, 5, 8, …
bullets: Cross-check via Form 2: l = a_30 = 2 + 29 × 3 = 89.
Always cross-check with the other form when both are available.
slides.speaker_notes: Doing both forms is a great error-catcher and reinforces the equivalence.

slides.title: Arithmetic mean
bullets: Three numbers x, m, y are in AP iff m = (x + y)/2.
Insert n means between a and b: total (n + 2) terms, so d = (b − a)/(n + 1).
Example: insert 3 means between 4 and 24 → d = 5; means 9, 14, 19.
Equal-step interpolation between two readings.
slides.speaker_notes: Keep a hand-drawn diagram of the (n + 2)-term AP for the inserted-means example.

slides.title: Word problems — four-step recipe
bullets: Step 1: identify the quantity that changes by a constant amount.
Step 2: read off a and d (or l).
Step 3: pick the right formula — a_n for a single term, S_n for a total.
Step 4: solve and reject any non-natural-number value of n.
Always sanity-check the surviving answer in the original problem.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress step 4 — students often miss that 'number of months' must be a positive integer.

slides.title: Word problem — savings
bullets: Savings: ₹100 in month 1, ₹125 in month 2, ₹150 in month 3, ….
AP with a = 100, d = 25.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through both forms of S_n to reinforce the cross-check habit.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 1. Find the 25th term of the AP −7, −4, −1, 2, ….
2. Find the sum of the first 100 odd natural numbers.
3. Insert 5 arithmetic means between 1 and 19.
4. The first row of an auditorium has 18 seats and each row 3 more. How many seats in 12 rows?
Compare answers with your bench partner.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk the room. Watch for the (n − 1) slip and for sum-vs-term confusion.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. Is 7, 7, 7, 7 an AP?
Q2. The common difference of 50, 47, 44, 41 is …
Q3. The 10th term of an AP with a = 4 and d = −2 is …
Show your answers on fingers (1 = first option …).
slides.speaker_notes: Use show-of-fingers to gauge the room. Address the question with the most disagreement.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: AP: sequence with constant d = a_2 − a_1 = a_3 − a_2 = ….
n-th term: a_n = a + (n − 1) d.
Sum of n terms: S_n = (n/2)(2 a + (n − 1) d) = (n/2)(a + l).
Arithmetic mean: (a + b)/2; insert n means with d = (b − a)/(n + 1).
Word problems: identify a, d (or l), pick the right formula, solve, reject non-natural n.
slides.speaker_notes: End with the 5 takeaways. Hand out the worksheet and announce the homework prompts.
